title: The Fall of Constantinople: The Last Day of the Roman Empire
youtube_title: The Fall of Constantinople: The Last Day of the Roman Empire | Full Documentary
description:
In 1453, a 21-year-old sultan brought giant cannon, and even dragged warships over a hill, to take the greatest city in Christendom. This is the story of the fifty-three-day siege, the last emperor of the Romans, and the morning an empire more than a thousand years old came to an end.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #constantinople #byzantine #ottoman #1453

beats.say: It is the early hours of Tuesday, May 29, 1453.
Outside the land walls of Constantinople, drums and trumpets tear through the dark.
Inside, church bells ring across the city.
For fifty-three days, a small garrison has held back one of the largest armies of its age.
Now the walls are broken in places, patched with barrels, earth and timber.
On those walls stands a man who calls himself Emperor of the Romans.
By sunrise, his city will fall.
And an empire that traced its line back more than eleven hundred years to Constantine the Great will come to an end.

show.title: A City of a Thousand Years

beats.say: To understand what was lost that morning, we have to go back to the year 330.
That year, the emperor Constantine the Great dedicated a new capital for the Roman Empire, on the old Greek town of Byzantium.
It sat on a triangle of land between two seas, where Europe meets Asia.
He named it after himself: Constantinople.
In the four hundreds, the western half of the empire collapsed.
Rome itself was sacked.
But the eastern half carried on, ruled from Constantinople, for another thousand years.
Today we call it the Byzantine Empire.
That name was invented by a German scholar in 1557, a century after the fall.

show.label: WHAT THEY CALLED THEMSELVES
show.sub: Rhomaioi · the empire of the Romans

beats.say: Its own people never used it.
They called themselves Romans, and their ruler was the Emperor of the Romans.
Their capital was protected by some of the strongest walls ever built.
On the land side, the Theodosian Walls ran for almost six kilometers, from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn.
They were built in the four hundreds: a moat, an outer wall, and a taller inner wall behind it.
Avars, Persians, Arabs, Rus and Bulgars all came against the city over the centuries.
The walls held them off.
At the heart of the city stood Hagia Sophia, finished in 537, for centuries the largest church in the Christian world.
But by 1453, the glory was mostly memory.
In 1204, crusaders from the West had broken in from the harbor side and sacked the city.
The empire never recovered.
By now it was little more than the capital, a few Aegean islands, and lands in southern Greece.
All around it spread a young, rising power: the Ottoman Turks.
Their capital, Edirne, lay only a few days' march away.
And in 1451, a new sultan took the throne there.
His name was Mehmed.
He was born in 1432, the son of Sultan Murad the Second.
He had already sat on the throne once, at just twelve years old.
That first reign did not last, and his father came back to rule.
When Murad died in 1451, Mehmed returned to power, still a teenager.
Many in Europe thought he would be weak.
They were wrong.
His aim was clear from the start: Constantinople.
In 1452, he built a fortress on the European shore of the Bosphorus, just north of the city.
Today it is called Rumeli Hisarı.
Its first name was Boğazkesen.
It means “Throat Cutter.”
From its walls, Ottoman guns could control the ships that fed the city from the Black Sea.
Across the water, the emperor watched.
Constantine the Eleventh was born in 1404, and crowned at Mistra in southern Greece in 1449.
He knew he could not win alone.
So he turned to the Christian West.
In December 1452, a Catholic service was held in Hagia Sophia, honoring the pope, in the hope of union with Rome and help from the West.
Many Orthodox citizens were furious.
And the help that came was small.
Venetian ships and crews in the harbor stayed to fight.
A Genoese soldier named Giovanni Giustiniani arrived with about seven hundred men, and took command of the land walls.

show.label: THE ODDS IN 1453
show.sub: defenders, against an Ottoman army many times larger

beats.say: Still, the numbers were brutal.
Modern estimates of the Ottoman army vary widely, but many land somewhere near a hundred thousand men.
Western eyewitnesses claimed far more, from 160,000 to 300,000.
The defenders numbered fewer than eight thousand, to guard walls that ran for miles.
And Mehmed was bringing something the walls had never faced.
A few months before the siege, a cannon maker named Orban came to Constantinople.
He was from Transylvania, in the Kingdom of Hungary.
He offered his services to the emperor.
But Constantine could not afford his fee, or the metal he needed.
So Orban went to Mehmed instead.
The sultan gave him everything he asked for.

show.label: ORBAN’S GREAT GUN
show.sub: long, firing stone balls said to weigh over half a ton

beats.say: At Edirne, over the winter, Orban cast a monster.
By most accounts it was about eight meters long.
Its stone balls are said to have weighed more than half a ton.
The exact figures vary from source to source.
Reports say it took sixty oxen and around two hundred men to haul it toward the city.
On April 6, 1453, the siege began.
The great gun and many smaller cannon pounded the land walls, day after day.
It was slow.
It could only fire a handful of times a day, perhaps as few as seven, because the barrel grew so hot.
One story says a great gun later burst, and that Orban may have died in the blast, but that is not certain.
Yet the damage was real.
Stretches of the ancient walls came crashing down.
The Venetian Nicolò Barbaro, a ship's surgeon inside the city, kept a diary through the siege.
He described how the defenders worked through each night to fill the gaps.
They used barrels packed with stones and earth, and banks of timber and branches soaked in water.
By morning, the breach was sealed again.
The walls bent.
They did not break.
So Mehmed turned his eyes to the sea.
On the north side of the city lay a deep harbor called the Golden Horn.
Its sea walls were weaker than the great land walls.
So the defenders stretched a chain across its mouth, floating on logs, from the city to Galata on the far shore.
The Ottoman fleet could not get in.
On April 20, four Christian ships fought their way through the Ottoman fleet and slipped inside the harbor.
It was a humiliation for the sultan.
Two days later, he answered with one of the boldest moves in military history.
Behind Galata, his men built a road up and over the hill.
They laid down wooden runways and greased them.
Then, on April 22, they hauled warships out of the Bosphorus, onto land, and over the hill.
Crews sat at the oars.
Sails were raised.

show.text: It was a strange spectacle, and unbelievable in the telling except to those who actually did see it – the sight of ships borne along on the mainland as if sailing on the sea.
show.who: KRITOBOULOS · HISTORY OF MEHMED THE CONQUEROR (TR. RIGGS)

beats.say: The Greek historian Kritoboulos, who later served the sultan, described the scene.
Barbaro counted seventy-two of them.
Other sources give different numbers, but it was dozens of ships.
They slid down into the Golden Horn, behind the chain.
Now the harbor walls were under threat too, and defenders had to be pulled from the land walls to guard them.
A night raid to burn the new Ottoman ships ended in disaster.
Ottoman guns sank the leading boat, and its Venetian captain, Giacomo Coco, went down with it.
Food was running short.
And word came that no great relief fleet from Venice was on its way.
The city was on its own.
Underground, the danger grew too.
Ottoman miners dug tunnels toward the foundations of the walls.
The defenders dug to meet them, and fought in the dark below the earth.
On May 22, Barbaro wrote, they found a tunnel, threw fire into it, and burned the men inside.
Then came the omens.
On May 22, the moon rose in partial eclipse.
Days later, a thick fog covered the city, and some said a strange light was seen around the dome of Hagia Sophia.
Barbaro recorded an old prophecy: the city would not fall until the moon rose darkened at the full.
Many took the signs to mean that God had left them.
On May 28, the Ottoman camp fell quiet.
Mehmed had ordered a final assault for the next day.
That evening, the emperor and his court went to Hagia Sophia.
Greek and Latin clergy stood together, Orthodox and Catholic, after months of bitter quarrels.
Accounts say people wept and asked each other for forgiveness.
Then the defenders went back to the walls.
Shortly after midnight, the attack began.
First came irregular troops, sent to wear the defenders down.
Then came regular soldiers from Anatolia, wave after wave, at the broken walls near the gate of Saint Romanus.
The defenders threw them back.
Barbaro wrote that the dead lay so thick beneath the walls, forty carts could not have carried them away.
Last came the Janissaries, the sultan's elite troops.
Around dawn, Giustiniani was badly wounded.
Accounts differ on what hit him.
His men carried him from the wall toward the ships.
Barbaro, a Venetian with little love for the Genoese, accused him of fleeing.
Most historians see a man gravely hurt.
He died of his wounds a few days later, on the island of Chios.
But on the wall, the damage was done.
His soldiers saw their commander leave, and panic spread.
There is another famous story.
The Byzantine historian Doukas wrote that a small gate called the Kerkoporta had been left open, and that Ottoman soldiers slipped through it.
Doukas is the only one who tells it, and many historians treat it as a legend.
Either way, Ottoman soldiers were soon on the walls.
Their banners went up on the towers.
The city was lost.

show.text: The blood flowed in the city like rainwater in the gutters after a sudden storm, and the corpses of Turks and Christians were thrown into the Dardanelles, where they floated out to sea like melons along a canal.
show.who: NICOLÒ BARBARO · DIARY OF THE SIEGE (TR. MELVILLE-JONES)

beats.say: Barbaro saw what came next.
Mehmed had promised his soldiers three days of plunder, as was the custom of the time.
Some sources say he called a halt far sooner, perhaps on the first day.
Either way, the damage was terrible.
Tens of thousands of people, perhaps around thirty thousand, were taken captive and sold into slavery.
A few Venetian and Genoese ships broke the chain and escaped to sea, packed with refugees.
And one question hung over the burning city.
Where was the emperor?
No one knows for certain how Constantine the Eleventh died.

show.text: No one could hear any news of the Emperor, what he had been doing, or whether he was dead or alive, but some said that his body had been seen among the corpses.
show.who: NICOLÒ BARBARO · DIARY OF THE SIEGE (TR. MELVILLE-JONES)

beats.say: Barbaro wrote down the rumors he heard that day.
Barbaro also passed on a claim that the emperor had hanged himself.
Few historians believe it.
The most famous story says he threw off his imperial regalia and charged into the fighting with his last men, to die as a soldier.
Ottoman accounts say his head was cut off.
His body was never securely identified.
He was forty-nine years old.
Later, Greek folk legend said he never died at all.
An angel turned him to marble and hid him beneath the Golden Gate, where he sleeps, waiting to return.
Mehmed rode into the conquered city.
He went to Hagia Sophia and ordered it turned into a mosque.
On Friday, June 1, 1453, Muslim prayers were held inside.
Minarets were added soon after.
For nearly five hundred years, it served as one of the great mosques of Islam.
Mehmed made the city his new capital, and began to bring people back to repopulate it.
He took a new title: Kayser-i Rûm.

show.label: FROM 330 TO 1453
show.sub: from Constantine the Great to Constantine the Eleventh

beats.say: Caesar of Rome.
From the founding of the city in 330 to its fall in 1453 was eleven hundred and twenty-three years.
It began with an emperor named Constantine.
It ended with one too.
Many historians see 1453 as a turning point: the end of the Middle Ages, and a sign that the age of high stone walls was passing.
Today, long stretches of the Theodosian Walls still stand in Istanbul.
Scarred, patched and silent.
They held for a thousand years.
On one Tuesday morning in May, they were not enough.
